idea: A type-specimen drawing of a single lowercase 'g' in a classic serif, with thin leader lines labeling bowl, loop, ear, link, counter, x-height and baseline, captioned 'Every letter has a skeleton.' For people who can't stop noticing fonts: it shows that a letter is a built object with named parts.

An exploded cutaway of Gutenberg's adjustable hand mould, with the punch, copper matrix and molten type metal (lead, tin, antimony) labeled, captioned 'The machine that made the machines.' A nod to the overlooked invention that let movable type be cast quickly and to the same size.

A branching Indo-European family tree where each tip carries that language's word for night: nox (Latin), nyx (Greek), nakt- (Sanskrit), naktis (Lithuanian), Nacht (German), night (English), captioned 'Everyone here is related.' Historical linguistics as a family portrait, plus a quiet point about kinship.

A left-to-right chart of the letter A evolving from a Proto-Sinaitic ox head ('alp) through Phoenician aleph and Greek alpha to the Roman capital, with the rotation marked at each stage, captioned 'It was an ox once.' A true origin story that makes the alphabet feel alive.

A log-log Zipf's-law plot of English word frequency where the points fall on a near-straight line, with the top words labeled the, of, and, to, a, in, captioned 'Language obeys a power law.' For data people who like the idea that nobody plans language, yet it follows math anyway.

A precise plan of a Linotype keyboard, whose first two columns of lowercase keys spell out letters in rough order of frequency, captioned 'etaoin shrdlu'. Operators sometimes ran a finger down those keys to fill out a bad line, and the nonsense occasionally got printed in newspapers by mistake. An insider password for print and type nerds.

A clean Reed-Kellogg sentence diagram of Chomsky's 1957 example 'Colorless green ideas sleep furiously.', with the subject, verb and modifiers on their slanted lines. It shows that perfect grammar can carry no meaning at all, and it's a beautiful bit of linguistics history.

A hardcover book in three-quarter cutaway, with signatures, sewing, headband, spine, joint, gutter, fore-edge and endpaper labeled the way a patent drawing would, captioned 'Fully offline.' A love letter to the codex as a piece of engineering that never needs updating.

A large Braille cell with the six dot positions numbered 1 to 6, surrounded by a small grid of all 64 combinations, captioned 'Six dots. Sixty-four possibilities. Louis Braille, 1829.' A minimal, graphic tribute to a teenager's writing system (he was 20 when it was published) and to how much fits in a tiny space.

A map of Europe with a single dot at Mainz and lines spreading out to the cities that had printing presses by 1500, captioned 'Mainz, c. 1450. Everywhere, 1500.' It shows the first information explosion as an elegant network map.

The Van de Graaf canon construction drawn as fine compass-and-straightedge lines over a two-page spread, where crossing diagonals fix the margins and text block, with no caption. It's the hidden geometry of medieval page layout, and design people will recognise it.

A construction drawing of the interrobang, a question mark and exclamation mark overlaid on a measured grid, captioned '‽ Martin K. Speckter, 1962.' The punctuation mark the world never adopted, for people who are always asking and exclaiming at once.

A side cross-section of the human head showing lips, teeth, alveolar ridge, hard palate, velum, tongue and glottis, with places of articulation marked bilabial to glottal, captioned 'Every word you have ever said happened here.' Anatomy and phonetics meet in a striking scientific illustration.

An outline schematic of the Rosetta Stone with its three registers labeled Hieroglyphic, Demotic and Ancient Greek, captioned 'Same decree, three scripts. 196 BC.' A celebration of translation as the key that let Champollion decipher hieroglyphs in 1822.

A top-down plan of a pair of compositor's type cases, the upper case holding capitals and the lower case holding small letters, with compartments drawn to their traditional uneven sizes, captioned 'Upper case. Lower case. It was furniture first.' The literal origin of an everyday word, which delights anyone who likes etymology.

An annotated dictionary-entry diagram with callouts for headword, part of speech, etymology and definition, using Samuel Johnson's real 1755 entry 'Lexicographer: a writer of dictionaries; a harmless drudge.' Self-deprecating wit from the 18th century, set out as a technical spec.

A minimal world map with three marked origins, Mesopotamia, China and Mesoamerica, each with an early sign (a cuneiform wedge, an oracle-bone character, a Maya glyph), captioned 'Writing was invented at least three times.' The point of view: writing is a human idea that keeps getting rediscovered, not the property of one civilization.

A diagram tracing placeholder text to its source: Cicero's line '...neque porro quisquam est qui dolorem ipsum quia dolor sit amet...' with lines showing how it was cut and scrambled into 'Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet', captioned 'De finibus bonorum et malorum, 45 BC.' Designers will enjoy finding out the fake text is a mangled passage about pain.

A cutaway of a reed stylus pressing into a wet clay tablet, with the wedge-shaped cross-section and the resulting impression shown in detail, beside a few proto-cuneiform tally signs, captioned 'The first writing was mostly bookkeeping.' A true and slightly subversive origin: literature came after the accounts.

A measured spec sheet of the hyphen, en dash and em dash side by side on an em-square grid, with widths and uses noted (compound, range, break), captioned 'Three different marks. Use accordingly.' A typographic stance for the people who notice when someone gets it wrong.
